Revenue $67.8 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $61.04 billion (36.3% year-on-year growth, 11.1% beat) Adjusted EPS $5.28 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $4.87 (8.5% beat) Operating margin 20.5%, up from 11.6% in the same quarter last year Oil production in line with the same quarter last year Chevron's third quarter results drew a positive response from the market, reflecting outperformance versus Wall Street's expectations. Management highlighted that operational discipline and strong execution across both upstream and downstream segments were critical in achieving these results. CEO Mike Wirth pointed to Chevron's record crude throughput in refining and sustained U.S. upstream production, while Vice Chairman Mark Nelson emphasized the impact of AI-driven reliability improvements and debottlenecking projects. The company's expanded activity in Venezuela and the commissioning of new facilities also contributed to quarterly momentum. Looking ahead, Chevron's strategic focus is on expanding low-cost production, leveraging technology, and maintaining capital discipline. Management cited upcoming increases in Venezuela production, ongoing digital innovation—including AI for operational optimization—and an active exploration portfolio as key growth pillars. CFO Eimear Bonner noted, "2026 is proving to be an inflection year for AI, with more than $100 million in value capture to date." The company also expects evolving geopolitical and market conditions to shape investment priorities and operational flexibility. Management attributed the quarter's performance to robust operational improvements, portfolio optimization, and expanded resource access, while forward guidance is anchored in technology-driven efficiencies and disciplined capital allocation. Venezuela production expansion: Chevron secured new fiscal terms in Venezuela and is ramping up joint venture output, aiming to double production by 2031 through a self-funding, low-cost development approach. Management highlighted that all crude from these ventures will be marketed directly by Chevron, improving revenue control and reducing above-ground risk exposure. AI-enabled operational efficiency: The company is deploying proprietary artificial intelligence tools across shale, exploration, and refining. These solutions have reduced downtime, improved drilling success rates, and delivered over $100 million in value so far this year, with further scaling expected. Refining and chemical yield optimization: Management cited peer-leading refinery complexity and the use of proprietary catalysts, resulting in a 10% increase in distillate yields at major U.S. refineries. Debottlenecking initiatives have added capacity at key facilities, supporting record quarterly crude throughput and meeting market demand. Expanded exploration footprint: Chevron doubled its acreage over the past two years, entering 12 new basins and prioritizing regions along the South Atlantic Margin and Eastern Mediterranean. AI-driven basin assessments and real-time drilling optimization have accelerated prospect identification and improved exploration outcomes. Bakken operational and financial improvements: The restructuring of Hess Midstream contracts halved midstream tariffs, strengthening Bakken's competitiveness and operational flexibility. Management expects further gains through optimized development plans, long lateral drilling, and integration with advanced chemical technologies. Chevron's outlook centers on scaling efficient production, leveraging digital tools, and navigating market and geopolitical dynamics to sustain profitability. Technology-driven production gains: Management plans to increase Venezuela and Permian output through factory-style drilling and advanced recovery methods, while AI-powered optimization tools are expected to deliver ongoing cost savings and production efficiencies. These efforts are designed to extend asset life and sustain plateau production in key regions. Disciplined capital allocation: Leadership reiterated a commitment to maintaining low net debt, consistently growing dividends, and investing efficiently in both organic and inorganic opportunities. The company anticipates continued volatility in global markets, underscoring the importance of its balanced capital allocation framework to support long-term growth and shareholder returns. content: Chevron just blew past every analyst price target on the street after a blowout quarter fueled by record refining profits, but one model is flashing a sell signal with unusual conviction. Here is what the bulls are missing. The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Chevron (NYSE:CVX | CVX Price Prediction) is $189.50. That is about 19.5% below this morning’s price of $235.39. The stock is up 58.74% year to date. Our model rates it a sell with 90% confidence. These Dividend Paying Energy Superstars Are Ready To Rock Chevron’s fundamentals look strong. Our concern is valuation. The stock now trades above the consensus analyst target of $232.50, which means Wall Street’s own math has fallen behind the rally. Our model expects earnings to normalize as oil prices cool, so it places most of its weight on forward earnings power and less on what investors are paying today. Our target is well below where Chevron trades, and the bull arguments carry real weight. Upside could come from Project Kilby, the Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) power deal, or from Brent staying high for longer than forecasts assume. Treat our 24/7 Wall St. price target as one data point among many. The bull case below lays out how Chevron could beat our model. Over the past week Chevron gained 3.84%. It rose 15.17% over the past month and 21.4% over the past quarter. That run took the stock past its prior 52-week high of $234.08 and far above its low of $142.51. In this morning’s third-quarter report, adjusted EPS came in at $5.28, ahead of the $4.83 estimate. Revenue of $65.24 billion beat expectations and rose 35.4% from a year earlier. Diesel prices drove much of the gain, as Chevron and Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM) both reported sharply higher refining profits according to CNBC. U.S. downstream earnings reached $3.58 billion, up from $638 million. Brent averaged $97 per barrel, compared with $69 a year ago. Chevron captured $1.5 billion of Hess synergies six months ahead of schedule. It also hit its $3 billion structural cost target early. Project Kilby, a 2.67 gigawatt power agreement with Microsoft, is expected to earn “mid-teens returns” that do not depend on oil prices. That Kilby deal is a reminder that the AI expansion runs on power, cooling, and fuel supplied by names outside the chip sector (we covered seven of them in a free report here). Venezuela adds more upside through a planned $7 billion joint venture investment. Management also targets adjusted free cash flow growth of greater than 10% per year through 2030, and that target assumes lower commodity prices. Analysts lean bullish, with 20 Buy or Strong Buy ratings and just one Sell. The bull scenario reaches $243.89. This year’s earnings depend heavily on oil prices that have been pushed up by the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz. The EIA projected that Brent would fall to $89 in the fourth quarter of 2026 and $79 in 2027. At 22x trailing earnings, Chevron is priced for peak conditions to last. GAAP results also included a $160 million legal reserve and a $110 million impairment. In fairness, those charges are mostly non-recurring. Chevron also cut net debt by $7.8 billion in the quarter, which improves the balance sheet. In our bear scenario, the stock falls to $171.13. Exxon Mobil is the closest integrated rival and had the same diesel-driven quarter. Its adjusted EPS of $4.23 beat the $3.981 estimate. Even so, Exxon trades at a cheaper forward multiple than Chevron. ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP) shows what pure upstream exposure looks like, without refining. It also trades at the lowest forward multiple of the three. Both peers trade at a discount, which makes the 24/7 Wall St. price target look reasonable. Chevron’s higher yield partly explains its premium. Our 24/7 Wall St. price target is $189.50, with a sell rating and 90% confidence. The deciding factor is the premium multiple sitting on top of peak-cycle earnings. I would turn more constructive if Kilby reaches a final investment decision and Brent holds near current levels. If oil follows the EIA’s forecast lower, I would expect the stock to give back gains. At these levels, the risk-reward looks extended to me. They rest on Chevron continuing its current strategy as oil prices normalize. title: Exxon's Refining Profits Soared—Did Chevron Get the Same Windfall? - MarketBeat
content:
The biggest question for investors is not whether Exxon's refining business has been thriving thanks in large part to record crack spreads amid the Iran war, but how much of the earnings from these operations reached the company's bottom line, and how long that benefit is likely to last. Since competitor Chevron NYSE: CVX reported its Q3 2026 earnings results on the same day, it provides a useful point of comparison. Ultimately, Exxon's refining and marketing earnings have surpassed its upstream earnings, but the favorable mix may not continue forever. Exxon posted its largest year-to-date (YTD) refining operational performance ever, contributing to $17.5 billion in adjusted Q3 2026 earnings. Breaking down these earnings by segment shows just how dramatically refining has impacted the company's overall performance. The company's Energy Products segment includes its refining and marketing operations; this portion of Exxon's business reached $9 billion in adjusted earnings for Q3, more than double what it was last year at this time. Meanwhile, the company's upstream business, including its core exploration and production operations, came in at $7.3 billion in adjusted earnings for the quarter, down from $9.2 billion in Q2 2026. This decline was substantially wider than Exxon had indicated in its pre-earnings report. In other words, Exxon's Energy Products segment became the company's largest earnings generator for the company this quarter. While this has been a boon for the company, it leaves it exposed if fuel margins should fade. At the same time, the company still produced about 4.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day—though this is about flat on a sequential basis, it nonetheless indicates that there are not necessarily major issues with Exxon's upstream operations for investors to worry about. For this firm, production remained the largest contributor to overall earnings. Chevron's upstream operations generated about $5.7 billion in reported earnings for Q3, while its downstream operations (including refining) yielded $4.9 billion. title: Geopolitical Turmoil Fuels Chevron's (NYSE: CVX) Refining Windfall As Quarterly Earnings Crush Wall Street Targets - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Oct 31, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis, Politics Attacks on refineries across Russia and the Middle East sent global diesel prices surging, and Chevron (NYSE: CVX) was among the biggest beneficiaries of the resulting supply disruption. American refiners moved swiftly to fill the gap left by damaged foreign capacity, and Chevron’s plants ran at 98% of capacity while processing a record of just over one million barrels per day. The result was a refining profit figure that few analysts anticipated, with that segment alone generating $3.59 billion compared with just $638 million during the same period a year earlier. Overall downstream operations earned $4.93 billion for the quarter, more than four times the $1.14 billion the division produced twelve months prior. Those refining gains combined with stronger crude prices to lift Chevron’s total quarterly profit to $9.9 billion, roughly triple what the company earned in the year-ago period. Earnings per share came in at $5.06, a dramatic improvement from $1.82 a year earlier, while adjusted earnings of $5.28 per share cleared Wall Street’s consensus estimate of $4.89 with room to spare. Higher crude prices added further fuel to the quarter’s strong performance, with Brent averaging $97 per barrel against $69 during the comparable period, pushing upstream earnings to $5.7 billion from $3.3 billion. The surge in profitability translated directly into cash generation, with Chevron producing $16 billion in operating cash flow and $12 billion in free cash flow, up sharply from $4.9 billion in free cash flow a year earlier. Management deployed that capital on multiple fronts, cutting total debt by $3.5 billion during the quarter while sustaining share repurchases at $2.5 billion. Looking beyond North America, Chevron disclosed plans for significant additional investment in Venezuela, where its joint ventures are expected to commit $7 billion over the coming five years. Investors responded positively to the results, sending Chevron shares approximately 2% higher in premarket trading following the earnings release. The quarter underscores how geopolitical instability, far from being a uniform drag on energy companies, can generate extraordinary windfalls for integrated oil majors with large and efficiently run refining operations. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

title: 5 revealing analyst questions from Chevron’s Q3 earnings call - StockStory
content: Chevron’s third quarter results drew a positive response from the market, reflecting outperformance versus Wall Street’s expectations. Management highlighted that operational discipline and strong execution across both upstream and downstream segments were critical in achieving these results. CEO Mike Wirth pointed to Chevron’s record crude throughput in refining and sustained U.S. upstream production, while Vice Chairman Mark Nelson emphasized the impact of AI-driven reliability improvements and debottlenecking projects. The company’s expanded activity in Venezuela and the commissioning of new facilities also contributed to quarterly momentum. Is now the time to buy CVX? Find out in our full research report (it’s free for active Edge members). While we enjoy listening to the management’s commentary, our favorite part of earnings calls is the analyst questions. Those are unscripted and can often highlight topics that management teams would rather avoid or topics where the answer is complicated. Here is what has caught our attention. Arun Jayaram (JPMorgan) asked about Venezuela’s cost structure and risk management; CEO Mike Wirth explained risk is mitigated through strong contract terms and local engagement, while CFO Eimear Bonner confirmed costs are below $20 per barrel, with investments recovering quickly. Devin McDermott (Morgan Stanley) inquired about the TCO concession extension in Kazakhstan; Wirth said discussions are progressing, with narrowed issues and both sides seeking a competitive, mutually beneficial agreement. Neil Mehta (Goldman Sachs) questioned Bakken’s core status post-midstream restructuring; Vice Chairman Mark Nelson said reduced tariffs improve returns and flexibility, and Bonner detailed financial benefits, including higher ROCE and simplified reporting. John Royall (Piper Sandler) sought details on refinery catalyst innovations; Nelson described proprietary catalysts boosting distillate yields by 10% and ongoing AI integration to optimize future yields and reliability. James West (Melius Research) asked about AI’s enterprise role; Bonner outlined over $100 million in captured value and detailed AI’s deployment in operational optimization, exploration, and well design, with Nelson highlighting accelerated basin assessments and higher drilling success. Looking forward, the StockStory team will monitor (1) Chevron’s ability to sustain and scale Venezuela production under new fiscal terms, (2) ongoing implementation and results from AI-led operational optimization across upstream and downstream assets, and (3) progress in expanding the exploration portfolio and turning discoveries into productive assets.
